target.title: fix(skills): enforce byte-level cap on skill package downloads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where skill package downloads via `pipeline(response.body, file)` have no byte-level cap. A malicious or compromised ClawHub registry could return an oversized response with missing or large Content-Length and fill the disk before the `timeoutMs` guard fires.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add two layers of protection:
1. **Content-Length pre-check**: If the response declares a Content-Length exceeding 256 MB, reject immediately without streaming any bytes.
2. **Streaming byte counter**: A `Transform` callback tracks cumulative bytes during the pipeline. If 256 MB is exceeded mid-stream (e.g. chunked transfer encoding with no Content-Length), the transform calls `callback(error)`, meaning the boundary-crossing chunk **never reaches the file**.

256 MB was chosen to match `LOCAL_SKILL_CARD_MAX_BYTES` style from the same module.

## User Impact

None under normal operation. Legitimate skill packages (typically <50 MB) are unaffected. Oversized downloads are rejected with a clear error message.

## Evidence

- **Code change**: 2 locations — constant declaration + downloadFile body
- **Content-Length path**: If a registry returns `content-length: 536870912`, the download throws immediately:
  ```
  Download content-length 536870912 exceeds maximum allowed 268435456 bytes
  ```
- **Chunked path**: If a registry streams data without Content-Length, the `Transform` byte counter rejects at the boundary. The crossing chunk is never forwarded to the file.
- **Temp cleanup**: `finally { rm(tempPath, { force: true }) }` removes partial downloads after any error.

### Automated tests

9 tests in `install-download.test.ts` (7 existing + 1 Content-Length loopback + 1 chunked streaming overflow):

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  9 passed (9)
 Type Errors  no errors
```

### Real behavior proof — standalone script against real HTTP servers

```
═══ Proof 1: Content-Length pre-check ═══

  Server: http://127.0.0.1:37215/huge.bin
  Content-Length header: 536870912 (512 MB)
  ✓ Download content-length 536870912 exceeds maximum allowed 268435456 bytes

═══ Proof 2: Chunked streaming byte counter (no Content-Length) ═══

  Server: http://127.0.0.1:45559/huge-chunked.bin
  5 × 64 MB = 320 MB total (no Content-Length → chunked transfer-encoding)
  ✓ Download exceeded 268435456 bytes (268597720 received)
  File on disk: 268435456 bytes (exactly at cap)
  Boundary-crossing chunk (64 MB) was NOT written to disk
  Temp file cleanup: ✓

═══ Summary ═══

  ✓ Content-Length pre-check: Rejected oversized Content-Length
  ✓ Chunked streaming byte counter: Rejected at 256 MB, boundary chunk not written to disk
  Passed: 2/2
```

Proof script: `scripts/proof-download-byte-limit.ts` — exercises the identical byte-limit logic from `install-download.ts` against real `node:http` servers using native `fetch()`.

### Codex review remediation

The first implementation used `PassThrough.on("data")` which detected overflow **after** the boundary-crossing chunk had already been forwarded to the write stream. Changed to `Transform._transform(chunk, encoding, callback)` where `callback(error)` prevents the chunk from reaching the file. Added a chunked streaming overflow test to cover the undeclared-length path.

---

AI-assisted.

target.title: feat(line): wire base.allowlist config-edit adapter
target.body:
Closes #106637

## What Problem This Solves

Running `openclaw allow line <id>` — or the in-chat `/allowlist add|remove` command — against the LINE channel replies `⚠️ line does not support dm allowlist edits via /allowlist.` instead of editing the allowlist. A LINE operator can't add or remove a DM/group allowlisted user at runtime; they have to stop and hand-edit the config file, even though the `channels.line.allowFrom` / `channels.line.groupAllowFrom` fields already exist. LINE is the only DM/group channel with this gap.

## Why This Change Was Made

The core `/allowlist` handler refuses whenever a channel plugin has no `allowlist.applyConfigEdit` (`src/auto-reply/reply/commands-allowlist.ts:465`). Every other DM/group channel declares one: Telegram, Signal, iMessage and WhatsApp via `buildDmGroupAccountAllowlistAdapter`; Discord and Slack via the legacy variant. LINE's `createChatChannelPlugin({ base })` never wired it.

This PR wires `buildDmGroupAccountAllowlistAdapter` into LINE's `base`, matching the Telegram/Signal shape exactly — no hand-rolled logic:

- **DM + group + `all` scopes.** LINE stores both `allowFrom` and `groupAllowFrom`, so the non-legacy DM/group builder is correct (not the legacy DM-only variant Discord/Slack use).
- **Per-group overrides** via `createFlatAllowlistOverrideResolver` over `groups.*.allowFrom` — LINE group config is flat (no Telegram-style nested topics), so the flat resolver is the right one.
- **LINE-specific entry normalization** (stripping the `line:` / `line:user:` prefix) reuses the existing `lineConfigAdapter.formatAllowFrom`, so a `line:user:U…` entry and the bare `U…` resolve to the same list member.

No config schema change (the fields already exist) and no dependency/lockfile changes.

## User Impact

`/allowlist add dm <lineUserId>`, `/allowlist remove …`, and the `group` scope now edit `channels.line.allowFrom` / `channels.line.groupAllowFrom` at the correct account scope — same UX as every other channel. Behavior is unchanged for other channels and for LINE users who never issue the command.

## Evidence

All local — this is a config-edit surface, no LINE API involved.

target.title: refactor(gateway-client): expose request dispatch boundary
target.body:
Related: #96230

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-internal callers can observe a request result or a later `accepted` response, but cannot distinguish a failure before the request frame entered the local WebSocket transport from a failure after dispatch. That distinction is required before later restart-recovery work can make conservative retry or refund decisions without guessing from promise settlement.

This is the first independently reviewable dependency extracted from #96230. The original PR remains frozen while its behavior is split into ordered, narrower changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The protocol client is the only layer that owns the synchronous `socket.send(...)` boundary, so this adds an optional `onDispatched` observer immediately after `send` returns successfully and routes it through the existing callback-isolation helper. The package client and high-level `callGateway` wrapper forward the same observer without changing request frames, protocol versions, timeout/abort cleanup, reconnect behavior, or `onAccepted` response semantics.

The observer contract is intentionally narrow: it means the request frame was handed to the local WebSocket transport. It does not mean the Gateway/server accepted or processed the request. The request option type now lives in a dedicated small module and is re-exported from the existing protocol-client module, preserving import and structural type compatibility while keeping the oversized implementation files within the repository LOC ratchet. The equivalent `CallGatewayOptions` shape is expressed through the existing CLI option alias for the same reason.

This is a root-cause boundary fix: higher layers no longer need to infer whether transport dispatch happened. The gateway-client package is private and the new field is additive and optional. A consumer/test-double sweep covered the package export, OpenClaw facade, SDK transport, accepted-response caller, both affected request stubs, and the node-host bridge. The node-host bridge only forwards `timeoutMs` across its IPC boundary, so later recovery code must use `callGateway` or introduce a separate IPC dispatch acknowledgement rather than assuming this observer is available there.

Out of scope for this PR: Plugin SDK/session-state isolation, recovery persistence, `mainRestartRecovery` admission or ownership, bounded recovery, quarantine, and Doctor repair. In particular, this PR does not write any production recovery state.

## User Impact

There is no direct end-user behavior change. Existing callers behave exactly as before; later recovery PRs can use a precise local transport-dispatch fact instead of broad failure inference.

Risk is limited to an additive observer callback. It is not invoked when WebSocket send throws, observer exceptions are isolated from request settlement, and the callback must not be interpreted as server acceptance.

## Evidence

Focused TDD reproduction before implementation:

```text
expected "vi.fn()" to be called 1 times, but got 0 times
```

Complete affected test files after the LOC-neutral follow-up:

```text
Gateway client watchdog: 18 passed (18)
Gateway call wrapper:     119 passed (119)
```

Real behavior proof used an isolated OpenClaw gateway and the production `callGateway -> GatewayClient -> GatewayProtocolClient` path for an authenticated `health` RPC over a real loopback WebSocket:

```text

Callback ran before response resolution: true
Callback intentionally threw: yes
Request still resolved successfully: yes
```

The send-exception regression also verifies that `onDispatched` is not called when `socket.send` fails and that pending request state is cleaned up.

Repository and package gates:

```text

Gateway-client package build: passed, including generated declarations
Scoped lint: passed
Scoped formatting: passed for all 6 changed files
```

target.title: Memory/QMD: isolate mcporter sidecars per agent
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

QMD memory searches that bridge through MCPorter need one generated sidecar configuration and daemon identity per OpenClaw agent. At the same time, OpenClaw must not copy user-owned MCPorter definitions—especially remote endpoints or stdio definitions that carry authentication, lifecycle, logging, relative paths, or other user-controlled behavior—into agent state.

This updates the existing PR rather than replacing it, retaining the complete behavior matrix from the original work on top of current `main`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The QMD manager now discovers the configured MCPorter server first. Bare QMD stdio definitions are normalized into a generated per-agent configuration; definitions that need the original MCPorter config are kept external and invoked against their discovered source file.

That matches MCPorter's own precedence contract: explicit configuration, then project configuration, then home configuration. The dependency source inspected for this update is `../mcporter/src/config/path-discovery.ts`, `../mcporter/src/paths.ts`, and `../mcporter/src/config-schema.ts`.

## User Impact

- Different agents no longer share generated QMD/MCPorter sidecar state or daemon ownership.

target.title: fix(reply): strip newline/whitespace-separated leading NO_REPLY sentinel
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #103735. Follow-up to #30916 and #30955.

When a model emits `NO_REPLY` on its own line before the real reply body, the literal `NO_REPLY` token leaks to the channel. The existing `startsWithSilentToken` only catches glued-attached tokens (`NO_REPLYhello`), and `stripSilentToken` only handles trailing tokens — a newline-separated leading preamble falls through both.

## Root Cause

`startsWithSilentToken` uses a glued-attached regex requiring `(?=[\p{L}\p{N}])`. A newline-separated leading token (`NO_REPLY\n\nWait...`) is not detected. The parallel announcement path in `subagent-announce.ts` has the same gap.

## Fix

Add `startsWithNewlineSeparatedSilentToken` to the shared `tokens.ts` module. The function matches a leading sentinel separated from substantive word content by at least one newline — the model-emitted preamble pattern — while preserving single-space-separated natural-language text (`NO_REPLY is the documented sentinel`).

Apply the shared detection to **both** callers:
- `normalize-reply.ts` — normal reply delivery
- `subagent-announce.ts` — subagent announcement delivery (parallel path identified by ClawSweeper)

## Files Changed

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/auto-reply/tokens.ts` | New `startsWithNewlineSeparatedSilentToken` export + shared regex |
| `src/auto-reply/tokens.test.ts` | 3 new tests for the shared function |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/normalize-reply.ts` | Replace inline `\s+` logic with shared function call |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/reply-utils.test.ts` | Updated test expectations (space-separated is now preserved) |
| `src/agents/subagent-announce.ts` | Added newline-separated detection (parallel announcement path) |

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof — OpenClaw main + PR patch, live Node.js import

```
$ node --import tsx/esm -e "import { startsWithNewlineSeparatedSilentToken } from '...'"

✅ Newline preamble:    "NO_REPLY\n\nWait"         → true  (detected)
✅ Single newline:      "NO_REPLY\nWait"           → true  (detected)
✅ Padded + newline:    "  NO_REPLY  \n\nAnswer"   → true  (detected)
✅ Space-separated:     "NO_REPLY is the sentinel" → false (preserved)
✅ Double dash:         "NO_REPLY -- nope"         → false (preserved)
✅ Punctuation:         "NO_REPLY: explanation"     → false (preserved)
✅ Glued (existing):    "NO_REPLYhello"            → false (handled by startsWithSilentToken)
✅ Trailing (existing): "Hello NO_REPLY"           → false (handled by stripSilentToken)
```

### Mantis Telegram Desktop Proof

Mantis captured Telegram before/after GIFs: leading `NO_REPLY` preamble removed, substantive reply preserved.

target.title: feat: configurable diagnostics.laneWaitWarnMs threshold
target.body:
## Summary

`diagnostics.laneWaitWarnMs` is now configurable. The "lane wait exceeded" warning's 2-second floor was hard-coded, so contended lanes flooded the diagnostic log even when waits were within normal operating range. The default stays at 2_000 ms; users on chatty lanes can raise it.

What problem does this PR solve? The `lane wait exceeded` line at `command-queue.ts` fires every time a queued task waits longer than 2 seconds for its lane, and there was no way to raise that floor without patching source.

Why does this matter now? Filed in #14747. On contended lanes, the 2-second floor produces noise that buries the actual stuck-lane signals.

What is the intended outcome? Operators can set `diagnostics.laneWaitWarnMs` in `openclaw.json` to a value that matches their environment. Default behavior unchanged when the field is absent.

What is intentionally out of scope? The lane-stagger and stuck-session thresholds. Those have their own config fields and should stay separately tunable.

What should reviewers focus on? The `resolveDefaultLaneWaitWarnMs()` fallback to the existing 2_000 ms constant when the runtime config snapshot has no `diagnostics` block, and the per-entry `warnAfterMs` capture so the diagnostic line tells you which threshold fired.

## Linked context

Closes #14747

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

- Behavior or issue addressed: The `diag.warn("lane wait exceeded: ...")` line at `command-queue.ts` must honor `diagnostics.laneWaitWarnMs` from the runtime config snapshot, default to 2_000 ms when absent, and surface the resolved threshold via the new `warnAfterMs=` field on the log line.
- Real environment tested: macOS 25.3.0 (Darwin), Node 26.0.0, pnpm 11.2.2. Built openclaw at this branch (cherry-picked the patch onto a workspace already at commit `c54a3a13eb` -- combined commit `ca381d0aa6`) via `pnpm install && pnpm build`. The harness imports the built artifacts at `dist/command-queue-Flr5BAJS.js` and `dist/runtime-snapshot-D93_HOsR.js` directly -- it runs the real bundled code, not the vitest source.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:
  1. `pnpm build` produced `dist/command-queue-Flr5BAJS.js`
  2. Wrote a small harness script that imports the built command-queue and runtime-snapshot modules, sets the runtime config snapshot to either no `diagnostics` block (default) or `{diagnostics: {laneWaitWarnMs: 100}}`, then enqueues two tasks on `test-lane` where Task A sleeps 500ms and Task B is enqueued immediately behind it (so Task B waits ~500ms for the lane)
  3. `node /tmp/lane-wait-test.mjs`
  4. The harness lives at: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mvanhorn/openclaw/evidence/86676/lane-wait-test.mjs
- Evidence after fix (screenshot, recording, terminal capture, console output, redacted runtime log, linked artifact, or copied live output):

  Live stdout captured from the harness against the real built modules (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mvanhorn/openclaw/evidence/86676/lane-wait-output.txt):

  ```
  === Default threshold (2000ms - warn should NOT fire): diagnostics.laneWaitWarnMs=undefined ===
    task A: A done, task B: B done

  === Custom threshold 100ms (warn SHOULD fire on Task B): diagnostics.laneWaitWarnMs=100 ===
  [diagnostic] lane wait exceeded: lane=test-lane waitedMs=502 warnAfterMs=100 queueAhead=0 activeAhead=1 activeNow=0 queueBehind=0
    task A: A done, task B: B done
  ```

- Observed result after fix:
  - When `diagnostics.laneWaitWarnMs` is unset, Task B waits ~500 ms which is under the 2_000 ms default fallback, so the `diag.warn("lane wait exceeded: ...")` line does NOT fire. Both tasks complete silently. Default behavior unchanged.
  - When `diagnostics.laneWaitWarnMs` is set to 100, Task B's 502 ms wait exceeds the configured threshold, so the warn line fires. The line carries the new `warnAfterMs=100` field this PR adds, so an operator reading the diagnostic stream can see which threshold fired (vs the silent hard-coded 2_000 ms before).
  - The resolved `warnAfterMs` in the log line matches the configured threshold exactly, confirming `resolveDefaultLaneWaitWarnMs()` reads `getRuntimeConfigSnapshot().diagnostics?.laneWaitWarnMs` correctly.
- What was not tested: Dynamic config-update path (changing the threshold while the gateway is live). The vitest in `command-queue.test.ts` covers the dynamic case but the live harness only proves the static-resolution path. The runtime snapshot is shared across both paths, so the runtime read is the same; the only thing not exercised live is the snapshot-change observer.
- Proof limitations or environment constraints: The harness exercises the built command-queue against a synthetic lane, not lane traffic from a real channel-driven workload. The lane code path is identical regardless of caller, and the threshold logic is in `command-queue.ts` itself (not in any caller-specific layer).
- Before evidence (optional but encouraged): On `main` before this patch, `command-queue.ts` had a hard-coded `2_000` literal at the warn-after site. There was no `warnAfterMs=` field in the log line, and no `diagnostics.laneWaitWarnMs` reader in `resolveDefaultLaneWaitWarnMs()` (the function did not exist).

## Tests and validation

Which commands did you run? Real harness against built artifacts (above) + `pnpm vitest run src/process/command-queue.test.ts` (3 new cases pass: per-entry threshold, default fallback, dynamic runtime-config update).

What regression coverage was added or updated? `src/process/command-queue.test.ts` got 3 new cases.

## Changes

- `src/config/zod-schema.ts`: adds `diagnostics.laneWaitWarnMs: z.number().int().positive().optional()`
- `src/config/schema.labels.ts`: documents the new field
- `src/process/command-queue.types.ts`: extends `CommandQueueRuntimeConfig` with the diagnostics shape
- `src/process/command-queue.ts`: adds `resolveDefaultLaneWaitWarnMs()` reading `getRuntimeConfigSnapshot().diagnostics?.laneWaitWarnMs` with a 2_000 ms fallback; carries the resolved value as `warnAfterMs` into the diagnostic line
- `src/process/command-queue.test.ts`: 3 new cases (per-entry threshold, default fallback, dynamic runtime-config update)
- `docs/gateway/diagnostics.md`: documents the new field, default, and reset semantics

Fixes #14747

## Summary

- **Problem**: After codex/CLI runtime turns where `deriveSessionTotalTokens()` can't derive a fresh total, `updateSessionStoreAfterAgentRun` unconditionally set `totalTokens` to `undefined` — dropping the previously valid session entry value. `/status` showed `?/272k` instead of the preserved total, oscillating back only after compaction.

- **What changed**: One `else` → `else if { preserve entry.totalTokens } else { undefined }` in `session-store.ts:252-262`.
- **What did NOT change**: No external API, no config, no Gateway behavior, no schema. `totalTokensFresh: false` is still set when the value is preserved — only compaction or explicit usage data stamps a fresh total.

Fixes #107324

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: After any codex/CLI runtime turn where per-turn totalTokens can't be derived, `/status` displayed `?/N` instead of the last known good value — the existing total was silently dropped.

target.title: fix(cron): skip deleteAfterRun and preserve counters for manual runs (#83538)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw cron run` (a manual/operator run) on a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot ("at") job used to delete the job on success — consuming the one-shot so its scheduled fire never happened (issue #83538). Manual runs also mutated `consecutiveErrors` / `consecutiveSkipped` counters and `nextRunAtMs`, corrupting the scheduled retry/backoff/next-run state that only real scheduler executions should own.

The root cause is that `applyJobResult()` had no notion of *who* triggered a run: manual, scheduled (timer), and the gateway on-exit watcher all shared one finalization path, so `shouldDelete` and the counter mutations fired for every successful run regardless of origin.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix threads an explicit `CronRunOrigin` (`"timer" | "watcher-terminal" | "operator"`) through cron finalization. `applyJobResult` derives `consumesOneShot` and `ownsSchedulerState` as `origin !== "operator"` and records `lastRunWasManual = origin === "operator"`, so operator runs record the outcome only (never consume a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot, never touch scheduler counters / `nextRunAtMs` / enabled state), while `timer` and `watcher-terminal` runs keep consuming and owning scheduler state — preserving the merged on-exit `deleteAfterRun` contract from #104550.

`origin` is kept strictly internal. It is **not** part of the public `CronServiceRunOptions`: exposing it there would let any in-process facade caller (plugin SDK, RPC handlers, tests) request `watcher-terminal` semantics and delete one-shots or mutate scheduler-owned counters/backoff/timing. Instead, the public `run` is always operator semantics, and the gateway on-exit watcher — the only legitimate non-operator caller, which already holds the concrete `CronService` instance — uses a concrete-only `CronService.runOnExitTerminal` entry (absent from `CronServiceContract` / `GatewayCronServiceContract`) to get consuming behavior. The invalid-persisted-run path (`skipInvalidPersistedManualRun`) also forwards the true caller origin instead of hard-coding `operator`, so an invalid watcher-terminal run keeps scheduler-owned semantics.

## User Impact

- Debugging/manually running a scheduled `deleteAfterRun` job no longer silently cancels its upcoming scheduled fire.
- Manual runs no longer corrupt retry backoff, auto-disable, or next-run timing of scheduled jobs.
- Gateway on-exit watcher-terminal one-shots continue to be consumed exactly as before (no regression for the #104550 contract).
- The scheduler-consuming origin is no longer reachable through the public cron API, so plugins/RPC/tests cannot accidentally (or intentionally) delete one-shots or mutate scheduler state via `run`.

## Evidence

Real-setup proof at the current head using a **real running OpenClaw gateway process and the real `openclaw cron` CLI** (not a vitest/function harness). Built from this head and run inside a `node:24-bookworm` container (container node v24.18.0; the repo engines floor is 24.15.0), against a real on-disk cron store (sqlite).

```
Head: c071ce7ca34e7a41e4fafab4a8863960fb9403c7
Gateway: OpenClaw 2026.7.2 (c071ce7)   dist/build-info.json commit = c071ce7c...

Built-artifact fix verification (fix compiled into the running gateway):
  dist/server-cron-*.js contains:
    async runOnExitTerminal(id, payload) { ... }
    run: (jobId, payload) => cron.runOnExitTerminal(jobId, payload)
  'watcher-terminal' occurs only inside runOnExitTerminal; the public run path
  forwards no origin.

PART A — OPERATOR PRESERVATION (real `openclaw cron run`)
  $ openclaw cron add "partA-ok-preserve" --at "+2h" --command "echo ..." --delete-after-run
    -> id 3c309f88..., nextRunAtMs 1784045230759
  $ openclaw cron run 3c309f88... --wait
    -> {"status":"ok", exitCode 0}          (operator path, success)
  $ openclaw cron get 3c309f88...
    -> job STILL PRESENT, enabled:true, deleteAfterRun:true,
       nextRunAtMs 1784045230759 (UNCHANGED), lastRunWasManual:true,
       no consecutiveErrors / no backoff mutation
  => successful operator run did NOT consume the one-shot, scheduler state intact.

PART B — WATCHER-TERMINAL CONSUMPTION (real gateway on-exit watcher cycle)
  $ openclaw cron add "partB-onexit-consume" --on-exit "sleep 8; echo ..." \
        --command "echo ..." --delete-after-run
  # real gateway watcher armed + spawned the watched process (seen in ps):
  #   bash -lc sleep 8   /   sleep 8
  [cron] cron-exit: watcher armed { jobId: a27c2044... }
  [cron] cron-exit: watched command exited; firing job { exitCode: 0 }
  $ openclaw cron get a27c2044...      -> "cron job not found"
  $ openclaw cron list                 -> only the 2 PART A jobs remain
  $ sqlite3 .../openclaw.sqlite 'select job_id from cron_jobs'  -> 2 rows (no partB)
  => real on-exit watcher-terminal run DID consume/delete the successful one-shot.

OVERALL: PASS — driven end-to-end through a live gateway + operator CLI + real
on-disk store. Operator and watcher-terminal origins are cleanly separated, and
the scheduler-consuming origin is unreachable from the public cron API.
```

Unit/regression coverage at head: the public `CronServiceContract.run` preserves a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot (operator semantics, no scheduler-state mutation) even though it can no longer request another origin, `CronService.runOnExitTerminal` still consumes a successful on-exit one-shot, and invalid watcher-terminal runs keep scheduler-owned semantics while operator invalid runs stay operator-attributed.

target.title: fix(auto-reply): turn-level NO_REPLY substrate-leak suppression (buffer-until-final)
target.body:
## Summary

Closes the substrate leak that delivers agent reasoning text to operator chats when a `NO_REPLY` final follows leading `block`-kind payloads in the same turn.

## The leak shape

From the 2026-05-24 forensic (fleet-ops session `cf23b629`):

```
[block] "Inbox empty, no threads, no spawns. State clean."
[tool]  { …tool output… }
[block] "more reasoning"
[final] "NO_REPLY"
```

Previously the two `block` payloads were delivered to Telegram immediately, and only the final `NO_REPLY` was suppressed by `normalize-reply`. Operators saw ~140 overnight notifications of reasoning that should never have shipped.

## Why a flag-on-NO_REPLY approach can't work

A previous iteration tried: at `enqueue` time, set `hasNoReplyInTurn = true` when the payload is exact `NO_REPLY`, and skip subsequent blocks. That fails because **the flag is unset at the moment the leading reasoning `block` enqueues** — by the time `NO_REPLY` arrives and flips the flag, the leak has already happened.

## The fix: buffer-until-final

In `createReplyDispatcher`:

| enqueue call                      | New behavior                                                |
| --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enqueue("block", payload)`       | Normalize at call-time; push normalized into `bufferedBlocks` instead of `sendChain`. |
| `enqueue("tool",  payload)`       | Unchanged — tool results must flow to the agent loop.       |
| `enqueue("final", "NO_REPLY")`    | Drop the entire `bufferedBlocks`, fire `onSkip("silent")` for each, drop the final too. |
| `enqueue("final", real-text)`     | Flush `bufferedBlocks` in order onto `sendChain`, then deliver the final.            |
| `markComplete()` with non-empty buffer | Defensive flush: stream tear-down without a final must not silently lose reasoning. |

Block-payload normalization (`transformReplyPayload`, heartbeat-strip, response-prefix) still happens at `enqueue` time so semantics and ordering are preserved.

A new opt-out, `enableTurnLevelNoReplySuppression: false`, restores legacy deliver-each-block-immediately behavior for callers that depend on it. The default is `true`.

## Test coverage

`src/auto-reply/reply/reply-dispatcher.turn-level-noreply.test.ts` — 9 tests, all passing:

1. **The actual leak shape**: leading `block` then `final: "NO_REPLY"` → nothing delivered; `onSkip("silent")` fired.
2. Multiple buffered blocks before `NO_REPLY` → all dropped, all skips emitted.
3. Final is a real reply → buffer flushed in order, then final delivered.
4. Tool-kind payload between blocks delivers immediately even though final is `NO_REPLY`.
5. Final-only `NO_REPLY` turn still suppressed (legacy normalize-reply path preserved).
6. Defensive `markComplete` flush when no final arrives (stream tear-down).
7. Opt-out (`enableTurnLevelNoReplySuppression: false`) restores legacy behavior — the leak shape leaks; this test pins it.
8. `transformReplyPayload` still applied at enqueue time on buffered blocks.
9. `onSkip` fires per dropped buffered block (channel observability).

```text
✓ src/auto-reply/reply/reply-dispatcher.turn-level-noreply.test.ts (9 tests) 73ms
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  9 passed (9)
```

## Authority / lineage

- Substrate-leak forensic 2026-05-24, fleet-ops session `cf23b629` (root cause = ~140 overnight reasoning leaks to Todd's Telegram).
- HEARTBEAT.md "NO_REPLY = ONLY TEXT IN THE TURN" doctrine patched across 16 agent workspaces 2026-05-24 as immediate mitigation (the prompt-level rule); this PR is the gateway-side enforcement that keeps the leak suppressed even when an agent prompt drifts.
- Design direction from woodhouse msg-20260524-183651-3206538 (Path B in-line redesign, buffer-until-final).

## Risk

- Non-suppression path (`enableTurnLevelNoReplySuppression: false`) is byte-equivalent to the previous implementation.
- Default-on path differs from previous behavior in exactly one observable way: intermediate `block` payloads are deferred until `final` arrives. The flush path on real finals re-uses the original `dispatchNormalized` helper that wraps the existing `sendChain` promise. Tool-kind is untouched. `pending`/`onIdle` accounting is preserved (each flushed block increments `pending` and decrements on settle, identical to the unbuffered path).
- Worst case if the design has a bug: a real `final` with leading blocks would still deliver everything in order (test 3); the leak-shape case would drop the leak (test 1). The only new "lossy" path is the defensive flush on premature `markComplete`, which would otherwise lose reasoning entirely (test 6 pins it as deliver-not-drop).

## Files

- `src/auto-reply/reply/reply-dispatcher.ts` — buffer-until-final implementation + new opt-out option.
- `src/auto-reply/reply/reply-dispatcher.turn-level-noreply.test.ts` — new regression coverage.

target.title: fix(irc): disconnect on oversized inbound lines
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a broken or hostile IRC server could keep sending an unterminated line and make OpenClaw retain the growing input indefinitely while the channel remained connected.

## Why This Change Was Made

The IRC client now applies the protocol's existing 512-byte wire limit to both complete inbound lines and the pending unterminated record. The check reserves the terminating CRLF and measures UTF-8 bytes, then reports the protocol error and closes the socket before parsing oversized input.

## User Impact

IRC connections no longer grow memory without bound on oversized inbound records. Legal 512-byte lines, split socket writes, PING/PONG handling, and multibyte UTF-8 input within the limit continue to work.

## Evidence

- Real Linux TCP loopback server/client regression: a post-registration 1 MiB fragment without CRLF produced exactly `IRC inbound line exceeds the 512-byte limit`, closed the socket, and made the client not ready.
- Real TCP boundary control: a legal 510-byte PING payload split across two socket writes (512 bytes including CRLF) was delivered and received a PONG while the client remained ready.
- UTF-8 control: an oversized multibyte line was rejected by byte length rather than JavaScript character count.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/irc/src/client.test.ts` — 19 passed.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/irc/src/client.surrogate.test.ts` — 5 passed.
- `.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode local` — clean, no accepted/actionable findings.
- `git diff --check` — passed.

Remote Testbox evidence was not available in the authoring environment because neither Crabbox nor Blacksmith was installed; the socket evidence above uses real kernel TCP sockets rather than mocked transports.

target.title: fix(memory): hide QMD transport metadata from recalled content
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

QMD deliberately wraps snippets in location metadata such as `@@ -10,4 @@ (9 before, 0 after)`. Its MCP interface additionally prefixes each returned line with a line number. OpenClaw was returning both transport envelopes as `MemorySearchResult.snippet`, which let `memory_search` and Dreaming consume metadata as remembered prose.

This change parses the envelope at the QMD adapter boundary, keeps its useful structured line range, and exposes only document content.

Related: #106937
Related: #89444, #71030

## Why

The metadata is intentional QMD transport output and there is no QMD/MCP setting to disable it. Fixing the QMD adapter is preferable to patching QMD, adding a proxy service, or applying QMD parsing to backend-agnostic persisted recall.

The parser is deliberately conservative:

- only a valid QMD envelope at the beginning of a snippet is recognized;
- positive safe integer ranges are required;
- MCP prefixes are removed only when the complete body is consecutively numbered;
- ordinary numbered prose such as `12: text`, malformed headers, mid-snippet headers, and a second header in real content are preserved;
- explicit MCP `startLine`/`endLine` values retain their existing precedence over header-derived locations;
- cleanup occurs before UTF-16-safe snippet limits are applied.

Historical recall-store migration is intentionally out of scope. The shared recall normalizer remains backend-agnostic and does not parse QMD envelopes.

## User Impact

- `memory_search` returns clean recalled text for both direct QMD CLI and mcporter/MCP paths.
- Dreaming no longer stages QMD transport headers or MCP line prefixes from new recalls.
- Legitimate non-QMD recall content beginning with a diff hunk remains unchanged.
- Search mode, reranking, scoring, collection routing, and persistent mcporter behavior are unchanged.

## Evidence

**Validation Summary**
- QMD snippet parser unit tests: **13/13 passed** (all envelope variants, MCP numbering, edge cases)
- QMD manager integration tests: **159/162 passed** (3 flaky filesystem timing failures unrelated to changes)
- short-term-promotion tests: validated locally; CI will run full suite
- TypeScript compilation: verified via project build pipeline
- Loc-ratchet: short-term-promotion.ts reduced from 2876 → 2709 lines (well below 2871-line baseline)

## Live Real-Environment Proof

Proof head: `5714bf96da5c3f15184f267c270d19dfd2018a73`

Environment: Node `v22.23.1`, OpenClaw source at the exact proof head, a real local QMD index, and the persistent mcporter/QMD MCP service. Remembered document text and paths are redacted below; transport metadata and structured line results are retained.

### Direct QMD CLI

The real direct QMD query returned this raw transport shape:

```text
@@ -2,4 @@ (1 before, 53 after)
[document content redacted]
```

The patched `QmdMemoryManager` with `mcporter.enabled=false` returned:

```json
{
  "startLine": 2,
  "endLine": 5,
  "snippet": "[clean document content redacted]"
}
```

The snippet contained neither the `@@` envelope nor transport line prefixes.

### mcporter/MCP

The same real index through the persistent `mcporter call qmd.query` transport returned the numbered MCP envelope:

```text
3: @@ -2,4 @@ (1 before, 53 after)
4: [document content redacted]
5: [document content redacted]
6: [document content redacted]
```

The patched `QmdMemoryManager` with `mcporter.enabled=true` returned:

```json
{
  "startLine": 2,
  "endLine": 5,
  "snippet": "[clean document content redacted]"
}
```

The snippet contained neither the numbered MCP prefix nor the QMD envelope, while the header-derived structured range remained intact.

### Stored-Recall Safety

The shared recall normalizer no longer imports or invokes the QMD parser. A focused regression records backend-agnostic content beginning with `@@ -7,1` and verifies the marker is preserved in the stored snippet.

Both exact-head adapter probes used deterministic lexical retrieval through the real transport to avoid query-expansion nondeterminism. The isolated runner imported `QmdMemoryManager` from the detached proof worktree in `mode=cli`, with synchronization and watchers disabled. The live gateway and its `dist` were untouched, and the temporary worktree was removed afterward.

## Validation

Validated on the exact proof head above:

- Exact-head GitHub CI build: passed.
- `qmd-snippet.test.ts`: 13/13 passed.
- Full affected test selection (`qmd-snippet`, QMD manager, slug-path integration, and short-term promotion): 237/237 passed.
- Backend-agnostic leading-diff regression and the three existing slug-path integrations are included in that passing selection.
- Changed files: `oxlint`, `oxfmt`, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Secret/config audit: only memory-core TypeScript source/test files are present; no local configuration or credentials are included.

## AI Assistance

This patch was implemented with Codex assistance. The live PR, ClawSweeper findings, adapter boundary, dependency output, and exact-head behavior were independently audited before this revision.

target.title: fix(ai): record token usage on Responses early-abort (#100954)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Azure/OpenAI Responses streams that end early with `response.incomplete` (e.g. `max_output_tokens` reached, content filter) never send `response.completed`. Both Responses stream processors on `main` assign `output.usage` **only** inside the `response.completed` branch, so these early-terminated streams leave usage — and its cost — at zero, dropping the reported token counts (including partial cache-hit tokens) and their cost from telemetry and session accounting. This is the drift described in #100954.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `response.incomplete` event carries a full `Response` object with the same `usage` shape (`input_tokens` / `output_tokens` / `total_tokens` + `input_tokens_details`) as `response.completed`. The fix records that usage — **and computes its cost** — when the stream terminates early. Both Responses processors had the identical completed-only defect, so both are fixed:
- `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.ts`
- `src/agents/openai-responses-transport.ts`

Both `response.completed` and the new `response.incomplete` branch route through one terminal usage+cost path (map usage → `calculateCost` → service-tier pricing). Cost must run for the incomplete path too because session accounting sums `usage.cost.total` (`src/agents/sessions/agent-session.ts`); recording tokens without cost would still under-report. Stop-reason mapping and completed-only backfill stay specific to `response.completed`. The abort lifecycle already forwards a populated `output.usage` into the emitted error event, so no changes to the abort path or the generic `normalizeUsage` were needed.

## Single Billing Source of Truth

Per review feedback ([P1] "use one canonical terminal-usage helper"), the terminal usage/cost invariant now lives in **one** shared mapper — `mapResponsesTerminalUsage` in `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-terminal-usage.ts`, re-exported via `@openclaw/ai/internal/openai`. It performs the priced bucket split, `calculateCost`, and service-tier pricing. Both processors call it:

- The package processor's `recordResponsesTerminalUsage` writes the priced usage onto the package `AssistantMessage`.
- The agent transport uses a thin adapter that adds only the agent-local `reasoningTokens` field, which the normalized `Usage` type (`packages/llm-core/src/types.ts`) does not model — it is tracked separately by the agent usage accumulator and diagnostics. The shared mapper returns a `Usage`; the agent layers reasoning on top.

No billing logic is duplicated across the two processors, and the previous agent-side `as never` casts are gone.

## User Impact

Token usage **and cost** telemetry stay accurate when a Responses stream is cut short, instead of silently reporting zero. No change to normal (`response.completed`) streams or to provider defaults.

## Evidence

Regression tests drive a real `response.incomplete` event (carrying nonzero tokens, including cache reads/writes) through the actual stream processors with **no** `response.completed`, then assert both the token buckets and a nonzero computed cost:

- `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.test.ts` → **52 passed** (early-abort test asserts `usage.cost.total > 0` and exact per-bucket cost)
- `src/agents/openai-transport-stream.test.ts` → **331 passed** (same regression added for the sibling processor)
- `src/agents/usage.normalization.test.ts` → **10 passed**
- Type check (`tsgo` core) → clean on the touched files; LOC ratchet clean.

Note on live proof: a redacted real-Azure early-abort transcript would require forcing `max_output_tokens`/content-filter termination against a live deployment, which I can't capture here. The regression tests instead feed the exact SDK `response.incomplete` event shape (per the OpenAI Node `ResponseIncompleteEvent` → `Response.usage` contract) through the unmodified processors, so they exercise the real terminal code path rather than a mock.

Closes #100954

---

target.title: feat(discord): opt-in Discord Activities widget support
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Agents can render rich, interactive HTML widgets in the web Control UI, but Discord answers are limited to markdown, embeds, and components — there is no way to show an agent-authored HTML widget to a Discord user. Discord messages cannot embed arbitrary HTML at all, so the only supported route for real HTML-in-Discord is a Discord **Activity** (an app hosted in a sandboxed iframe inside the Discord client).

This adds an opt-in Discord Activities integration so an agent can post a widget that a user opens as an interactive Activity inside Discord.

## Why This Change Was Made

Requested capability: give the agent a way to surface interactive HTML to Discord users. The design constraints:

- **Off by default.** When `channels.discord.activities` is not configured, nothing changes — no HTTP routes, no agent tool, no interaction handler are registered. Zero new surface for existing users.
- **Easy to enable.** One config block plus documented Developer Portal + tunnel steps. When enabled, the `discord_widget` tool becomes available to agents in Discord sessions automatically (gated per account).
- **Transport-only channel.** Widget/session/token policy lives in the Discord plugin; core is untouched except for the additive config surface.

## User Impact

New, opt-in only. Once an operator configures `channels.discord.activities` (client secret + a public HTTPS route to the gateway, e.g. a Cloudflare Tunnel):

1. The agent calls `discord_widget` with self-contained HTML + a title.
2. OpenClaw stores the widget and posts a message with an **Open widget** button.
3. The user clicks it → Discord launches the OpenClaw Activity (`LAUNCH_ACTIVITY`, interaction callback type 12).
4. The Activity shell authenticates the user via Discord OAuth, checks them against the account allowlist, and renders the widget HTML in a nested sandboxed iframe.

Security model:
- OAuth identifies the Discord user before any widget metadata is returned; the user must match the account `allowFrom`/`dm.allowFrom` (open-DM accounts allow all, matching existing DM policy).
- The primary widget lookup is by an unguessable 22-char widget id carried in `custom_id` (a capability). The fallback, used only when Discord omits `custom_id`, resolves the channel from Discord's **Activity Instance API** under bot auth and verifies the requesting user is an active participant — a client-supplied channel id is never trusted.
- OAuth sessions expire after 15 minutes; widget document capabilities are single-use and expire after 60 seconds; widgets expire after 7 days (max 64 retained per plugin instance).
- Widget HTML runs under `sandbox="allow-scripts"` with a CSP that blocks all network access and external resources.
- The public token-exchange route is rate-limited per client IP, with a global budget charged only for well-formed, account-resolved exchange attempts so anonymous traffic cannot exhaust it.

Config keys (documented in `docs/channels/discord-activities`):
- `channels.discord.activities.clientSecret` — OAuth2 client secret (sensitive; falls back to `DISCORD_CLIENT_SECRET`).
- `channels.discord.activities.applicationId` — optional; defaults to the bot application id learned at startup.

## Evidence

- New agent tool `discord_widget`, HTTP routes under `/discord/activity` (auth: plugin, registered only when enabled), launch-button interaction handler, OAuth token exchange, session/widget/doc-token SQLite-backed stores, and a standalone Activity shell that bundles `@discord/embedded-app-sdk`.
- Config contract updated in lockstep: exported types, zod schema (client secret registered sensitive/redacted), help/labels, UI hints, generated bundled-channel metadata, and docs baseline.
- Docs: new `docs/channels/discord-activities` setup page (Developer Portal, Cloudflare Tunnel example, security model, troubleshooting) + config-key cross-links from `docs/channels/discord`.
- Tests: colocated `extensions/discord/src/activities/*.test.ts` cover config gating, tool execute (store + button + oversized/ fragment HTML), interaction launch/auth, OAuth happy/401/403/503, per-IP + global rate limits, session/widget/doc-token single-use, the Activity-instance channel resolution + participant check, and vendor-asset serving/fallback. Plugin-state `maxValueBytes` per-namespace limit added with tests. Bundled-plugin-assets + runtime-postbuild tests cover the new SDK build hook/static asset.
- Validation: `pnpm check:changed` + full `extensions/discord`, `src/plugin-state`, and touched `src/config` suites green on Blacksmith Testbox. Live smoke against a scratch gateway with the feature configured: shell `200`, bogus code `401`, unauth widget `401`, forged instance/channel with fake session `401`, vendor SDK asset `200` serving the real bundle. Autoreview (Codex gpt-5.6-sol) clean.
- The SDK browser bundle is a gitignored build artifact produced by `scripts/build-discord-activity-sdk.mjs` (mirrors the diffs-language-pack precedent).

Live-Discord items that still need real-client confirmation (documented in-page): whether `custom_id` propagates through `LAUNCH_ACTIVITY` (the Activity-instance fallback covers the case where it does not), and Developer Portal URL-mapping behavior.

target.title: fix(agents): keep max-turn context values UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`formatCliOutputError` emits a user-visible "Claude CLI stopped after reaching the maximum number of turns. OpenClaw run: <runId>. OpenClaw session: <sessionId>." error string for max-turns CLI failures. The internal `normalizeCliContextValue` helper used `String.prototype.slice(0, 200)` to bound the run/session context, so an emoji (or any other astral code point) landing at the 200th UTF-16 code unit left a lone high surrogate in the head. That surrogate was then propagated through `JSON.stringify` (used by the CLI streaming path) and rewritten to U+FFFD in the rendered error string, silently corrupting the user-visible attribution for any ID containing emoji or other surrogate-pair characters.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replaces the raw `slice(0, 200)` in `normalizeCliContextValue` with the shared `sliceUtf16Safe` helper from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice` (re-exported as `openclaw/plugin-sdk/text-utility-runtime`'s `sliceUtf16Safe`). The head now lands on the nearest UTF-16 code-point boundary so an emoji at the 200-char boundary is dropped instead of leaving a lone surrogate.

The three-argument form `sliceUtf16Safe(input, 0, 200)` matches `String.prototype.slice(0, 200)` semantics for inputs shorter than 200 chars (the two-argument form would treat `start=200` as an exclusive end and return "" for short inputs). This mirrors the canonical Wave 2 UTF-16-safe cohort (#102949, #104540, #104423) that introduced the same helper to Nextcloud Talk, persisted tool details, agents bootstrap, cron exec tails, agents block chunks, and agents context pruning.

`formatCliOutputError` exercises `normalizeCliContextValue` for `attribution.runId`, `attribution.sessionId`, and `output.sessionId`, so the fix covers all three context strings in one change.

## User Impact

`formatCliOutputError` now only emits heads that are valid UTF-16 code-point sequences. ASCII inputs (the common case for run/session IDs) are unchanged. Emojis or other astral code points that straddle the 200-char boundary are dropped back to the previous code-point boundary, producing a 199-char head instead of a 200-char head that would have been corrupted to U+FFFD by `JSON.stringify`. The same fix applies to all three context strings emitted by `formatCliOutputError`.

## Evidence

### Before fix (FAIL on pinned main `27d5c0339b8`)

```text
 FAIL  |agents| src/agents/cli-output.test.ts > parseCliJsonl > keeps max-turn context values UTF-16 safe when an emoji straddles the 200-char head boundary
AssertionError: expected 'Claude CLI stopped after reaching the…' not to match /[\uD800-\uDBFF](?![\uDC00-\uDFFF])|(?…/

- Expected:
/[\uD800-\uDBFF](?![\uDC00-\uDFFF])|(?<![\uD800-\uDBFF])[\uDC00-\uDFFF]/

+ Received:
"Claude CLI stopped after reaching the maximum number of turns (limit: 1). OpenClaw run: aaaaaaa…(199 a's)…. OpenClaw session: bbbbbbb…(199 b's)…. Claude session: session-utf16-boundary. Tool actions may already have run; …"

 ❯ src/agents/cli-output.test.ts:1050:27

 Test Files  1 failed (1)
      Tests  1 failed | 66 passed (67)
```

The lone U+FFFD replacement character was already in the rendered string at the time of the assertion (the `JSON.stringify` round-trip in the same test would have rewritten the lone high surrogate to U+FFFD).

### After fix (PASS on patched head)

```text
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  67 passed (67)
   Duration  969ms (transform 510ms, setup 523ms, import 76ms, tests 156ms, environment 0ms)

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 7.68s
```

### Focused regression

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/cli-output.test.ts` — 67/67 passed (66 existing + 1 new `keeps max-turn context values UTF-16 safe when an emoji straddles the 200-char head boundary`).
- The new test asserts (1) the formatted error contains no lone surrogate, (2) the head ends on a code-point boundary, (3) both `runId` and `sessionId` are trimmed to 199 ASCII chars when the emoji straddles index 200, and (4) the result round-trips through `JSON.stringify` without forcing any surrogate to U+FFFD.
- `git diff --check` — clean.
- `git diff --numstat` — `66 / -1` across `src/agents/cli-output.test.ts` and `src/agents/cli-output.ts`.

### What was NOT changed

- `openclaw/plugin-sdk/number-runtime` / `text-utility-runtime` / `utf16-slice` — the shared helper is used as-is.
- The 200-char cap (still 200 ASCII chars or 199 when the boundary lands inside an astral code point).
- `formatCliOutputError` call signatures, error text, or wording.
- The `parseCliJsonl` / `parseCliJson` / `parseCliOutput` parsers, streaming helpers, or CLI backend config.
- The `CliOutput` shape, diagnostics, usage, or terminal failure contract.
- Any other max-turns / runId / sessionId consumer outside `src/agents/cli-output.ts`.

## Risk / Compatibility

The only observable behavior change is the head length: when the 200-char boundary lands inside an emoji or other astral code point, the head drops back to the previous code-point boundary (199 ASCII chars in the test fixture) instead of leaving a lone high surrogate that `JSON.stringify` would rewrite to U+FFFD. ASCII inputs (the common case for run/session IDs) are unchanged. The same 200-char cap and the same `formatCliOutputError` call surface remain in effect; the user-visible error wording, prefix/suffix structure, and filter behavior are unchanged.

- #104540 — `fix(sessions): prevent corrupted Unicode in persisted tool details` (xingzhou)
- #104423 — `fix(agents): preserve UTF-16 boundaries in bootstrap context` (mushuiyu886)

Closes #107447.

## What Problem This Solves

Full-auto Codex app-server command approvals can still be declined before execution when the native hook relay is missing or stale.

The failing shape is a runtime that should not require human exec approval: `approvalPolicy=never`, `sandbox=danger-full-access`, no network proxy, corresponding to OpenClaw `tools.exec.security=full` and `tools.exec.ask=off`. The approval bridge checked the native hook relay before honoring `autoApprove`, so relay unavailability could send Codex a decline decision and produce a pre-exec `status: declined` command item.

- Treat native hook relay unavailability as non-authoritative only in that full-auto path.
- Continue running the normal OpenClaw before-tool-call hook before auto-accepting.
- Keep explicit native hook denials blocking.

target.title: fix(zalo): bound proxy fetcher cache to 64 entries
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves
Fixes two issues in Zalo `resolveZaloProxyFetch`:

1. **Unbounded proxy fetcher cache:** The process-lifetime `Map` retained one `makeProxyFetch` entry per distinct proxy URL with no eviction, letting config churn or high-cardinality URLs grow gateway memory without limit.

2. **Orphaned Undici ProxyAgent dispatchers:** `pruneMapToMaxSize` dropped the fetch closure but left the underlying Undici `ProxyAgent` alive with keep-alive connections, so successful traffic through many proxy URLs could still retain more than 64 live agents.

## Why This Change Was Made
- Cap `proxyCache` at 64 entries using the shared `pruneMapToMaxSize` helper (same pattern as Nextcloud Talk / MS Teams / Mattermost caches).
- Add `PROXY_FETCH_CLOSE` symbol to `makeProxyFetch` in `src/infra/net/proxy-fetch.ts` so cache owners can gracefully close the lazy Undici `ProxyAgent` dispatcher when an entry is evicted.
- Export `PROXY_FETCH_CLOSE` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/fetch-runtime` for plugin use.
- Before pruning, resolveZaloProxyFetch closes the oldest entry's dispatcher via the symbol, then inserts and prunes.
- No new config/env surface. Does not change Bot API timeouts or other Zalo send paths.

Collision check: searched open PRs for `proxyCache`, `pruneMapToMaxSize zalo`, `PROXY_FETCH_CLOSE`, `zalo proxy`; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact
**Before:** Long-running Zalo gateways retained an unbounded number of proxy fetcher closures AND their underlying Undici ProxyAgent dispatchers (with keep-alive connections), regardless of Map eviction.

**After:** At most 64 distinct proxy fetchers with their dispatchers are retained; evicted entries have their ProxyAgent gracefully closed before the Map entry is dropped.

## Verification
- Exact head: `3504201717f`
- `oxfmt --check src/infra/net/proxy-fetch.ts src/plugin-sdk/fetch-runtime.ts extensions/zalo/src/proxy.ts extensions/zalo/src/proxy.test.ts` — All matched files use the correct format.
- `git diff --check` — passed; exit 0.
- Focused tests:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/zalo/src/proxy.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```
 Tests  6 passed (6)
```

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/zalo/src/proxy.proof.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```
 Tests  1 passed (1)
```

- Mutation check (Map eviction): temporarily removed `pruneMapToMaxSize` → standalone proof exits 1 with `oldest_evicted=false` → restored → passes.
- Mutation check (dispatcher close): temporarily removed the PROXY_FETCH_CLOSE block → closeSpy not called → test `closes the underlying ProxyAgent dispatcher on eviction` fails → restored → passes.

## Real behavior proof

### Standalone proof (outside Vitest)

```bash
node --import tsx proof-zalo-proxy-cap.mts
```

```json
{
  "max": 64,
  "filled": 65,
  "all_fetchers_callable": true,
  "proxy_tag_preserved": true,
  "oldest_evicted": true,
```

- Negative controls: both the Map eviction and the dispatcher close have executable mutation checks proving they are the sole defense.

What was not tested: live Zalo gateway with real Zalo credentials. The proxy cache bounding and dispatcher cleanup are in-process; the standalone proof exercises the same code path a running gateway uses.

## Risk / Compatibility

target.title: fix(ollama): stop oversized stream records from growing memory
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users connected to a malfunctioning or hostile Ollama endpoint could see OpenClaw memory keep growing when the endpoint streamed an arbitrarily large NDJSON record without a newline.

## Why This Change Was Made

The native Ollama parser now caps each pending NDJSON record at 16 MiB using the original response bytes, resets the count at every newline, and cancels the reader before reporting an overflow. The risk is bounded to individual records larger than 16 MiB; long streams made of valid smaller records remain supported, and this does not change request timeout behavior addressed by #96635.

## User Impact

OpenClaw now stops an oversized Ollama stream record with an actionable error instead of retaining unbounded response data in memory. Normal multi-record Ollama responses continue to stream as before.

## Evidence

AI-assisted.

Premise: Ollama documents streamed REST responses as newline-delimited JSON with the `application/x-ndjson` content type: https://docs.ollama.com/api/streaming. A request timeout does not bound a continuously arriving record that never reaches its newline delimiter.

Real machine / production-path proof used Linux 6.8.0-134-generic x86_64, Node v24.18.0, a real localhost `node:http` server exposing `/api/chat`, and the exported production `createOllamaStreamFn`. The server sent one 20 MiB JSON record in 1 MiB writes. The same temporary harness was run with:

```text
node --import tsx /tmp/ollama-ndjson-real-proof.mts
```

Negative control / before, latest `upstream/main` (`d6fc3d34e2010997d4f67807b30c336347808f31`) in a detached worktree: the client accepted the complete 20,971,644-byte record and returned its `ok` content.

```json
{"node":"v24.18.0","recordBytes":20971644,"bytesWritten":20971645,"responseClosed":true,"terminal":{"type":"done","content":[{"type":"text","text":"ok"}]}}
```

After, commit `296d1e03`: the same production path stopped at the 16 MiB record cap, surfaced the overflow, and closed the live HTTP response before the server finished its payload.

```json
{"node":"v24.18.0","recordBytes":20971644,"bytesWritten":19923066,"responseClosed":true,"terminal":{"type":"error","errorMessage":"Ollama NDJSON record exceeds 16777216 bytes"}}
```

Focused regression and controls:

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/ollama/src/stream-runtime.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  106 passed (106)
```

target.title: fix(gateway): evict oldest rate-limit bucket by window age, not insertion order
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`consumeControlPlaneWriteBudget()` uses `controlPlaneBuckets.keys().next().value` to pick a bucket to evict when the map reaches its 10,000-entry hard cap. The variable is named `oldest`.

`Map.keys().next()` returns the first key by **insertion order**, not the bucket with the **smallest `windowStartMs`** (i.e. the one whose rate-limit window is oldest by wall-clock time). These two orderings diverge because of how `Map.set()` interacts with the ECMAScript insertion-order guarantee:

- When `Map.set(existingKey, newValue)` is called for an **already-present** key, the value is updated but the key's insertion-order position is **left unchanged** (§23.1.3.9).
- Active buckets trigger `set()` during window resets (line 60), but they stay in their original insertion-order slot.
- Newer buckets inserted later can have genuinely older `windowStartMs` values while sitting behind the early-inserted but recently-reset active bucket.

This means an early-inserted, still-active bucket can be evicted while genuinely older (expired) buckets remain in the map. The active client's rate-limit state is lost, effectively giving it a free pass.

`pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets()` (line 99–108) in the same file already uses the correct criterion — it walks the full map and tests each bucket's `windowStartMs`. The eviction path should use the same criterion.

## Why This Change Was Made

The eviction path now scans the full map for the bucket with the smallest `windowStartMs` instead of trusting insertion order. This matches the intent of the variable name `oldest` and aligns with `pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets`.

The loop walks at most 10,000 entries (`CONTROL_PLANE_BUCKET_MAX_ENTRIES`), which takes < 1ms on a modern CPU. This path is cold: it only executes when a **new** client arrives while the map is already at its hard cap — a scenario that requires 10,000 unique device/IP combinations before it triggers even once. The cost is negligible and the path is identical every 1 in 10,000+ calls.

## User Impact

No user-observable API or config changes. The only affected scenario is a gateway under 10,000+ unique client identities — at which point eviction fairness improves: the bucket evicted is the one whose rate-limit window is actually oldest, not the one that was inserted first.

## Evidence

**Behavior addressed**: `Map.keys().next()` (insertion order) used as a proxy for `min(windowStartMs)` (age order) in control-plane rate-limit bucket eviction. The two orders diverge per ECMAScript §23.1.3.9: `Map.set(existingKey, val)` does not reposition the key.

**The semantic gap in code** — before (left) vs after (right):

```
BEFORE (keys().next()):                         AFTER (min windowStartMs):
                                                 
Map.set() does not reposition existing keys.    Iterates all buckets to find the one whose
An active bucket that resets its window         windowStartMs is numerically smallest —
many times keeps its original insertion-        i.e. the bucket whose rate-limit window
order slot.                                     started earliest, and is therefore the
                                                 closest to expiry or already expired.
keys().next() → oldest by insertion, not age.   
                                                 old variable name "oldest" → now correct.

pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets() already        pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets() uses the
uses windowStartMs (line 101).  The eviction    same criterion — the two paths are aligned.
path diverged from this criterion.
```

**Proof that `Map.set(existingKey, _)` preserves insertion order** — ECMAScript specification §23.1.3.9 `Map.prototype.set`:

```
4. Let p be the Record {[[Key]]: key, [[Value]]: value}.
5. If p is not present, append p to the end of the List.
   (No repositioning step for existing keys.)
```

**Focus test verification**:

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.test.ts --run
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.ts
exit 0

$ git diff --stat HEAD~1..HEAD
 src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.ts | 18 ++++++++++++++----
 1 file changed, 14 insertions(+), 4 deletions(-)
```

**Observed result**: All existing tests pass unchanged. The eviction path now selects the bucket with the smallest `windowStartMs` rather than the first key by insertion order.

**What was not tested**: A live gateway with 10,000+ unique device/IP identities exercising the eviction path. The pre-condition (10,000 unique clients) is a production extreme that is not practical to simulate in unit tests. The fix is verified through: (1) ECMAScript spec citation proving the old behavior was wrong, (2) alignment with the same file's own `pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets` pattern, (3) existing tests still pass.

## Root Cause

In `consumeControlPlaneWriteBudget()`, the hard-cap eviction path used `controlPlaneBuckets.keys().next().value` as a proxy for "oldest bucket." The variable was named `oldest`, indicating the intent was age-based eviction.

`Map.keys().next()` returns keys by insertion order, not by `windowStartMs`. Per the ECMAScript specification (§23.1.3.9), `Map.set(key, value)` for an existing key updates the value but does **not** reposition the key in insertion order. An active bucket that resets its window via `set()` stays in its original insertion-order slot; a bucket inserted later can have an older `windowStartMs` while sitting behind it in insertion order.

The same file's `pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets()` function already walks the full map and checks `bucket.windowStartMs` (line 101–102). The eviction path had inadvertently diverged from this criterion by using insertion order instead.

target.title: fix(sessions-send): normalize sourceSessionKey to dmScope-resolved canonical key
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When `session.dmScope` is `"main"` (default), inter-agent messages sent via `sessions_send` embed the calling session persisted storage key as `sourceSessionKey` — even when that key was created under a previous `per-account-channel-peer` routing regime. The receiving agent replies to the stale key, creating a ghost session that the sender never monitors, causing permanent one-way communication failure between agents.

**Split path:**
1. **Inbound user DMs** → resolved via `buildAgentPeerSessionKey()` with `dmScope="main"` → lands in `agent:{id}:main` ✓
2. **Inter-session replies** → routed to `sourceSessionKey` from provenance → lands in `agent:{id}:{channel}:{account}:direct:{peer}` (stale format) ✗

Two different session keys → two different sessions → the agent in session A never sees replies delivered to session B.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `sessions_send` tool passed `opts.agentSessionKey` verbatim into `inputProvenance.sourceSessionKey`. This is the session persisted key from storage, not a dmScope-resolved key. The fix normalizes the requester key through `buildAgentMainSessionKey()` when `dmScope` is `"main"`, so all downstream provenance, watch registration, same-session detection, and A2A ping-pong routing use the same canonical key that the agent actually monitors.

## User Impact

Multi-agent setups using `dmScope="main"` (the default) with sessions that predate a routing regime change will now correctly route inter-agent replies back to the sender monitored session. No config changes required. Operators with `dmScope` set to `per-peer`, `per-channel-peer`, or `per-account-channel-peer` are unaffected — the normalization only activates when `dmScope` is `"main"`.

## Evidence

- `sessions-send-helpers.test.ts`: **10/10 passed**
- `sessions-send-tool.a2a.test.ts`: **25/25 passed**
- oxfmt and git diff --check clean

Fixes #107399

  ```bash
      --edenai-api-key "$EDENAI_API_KEY"
  pnpm openclaw models list --provider edenai | head
  pnpm openclaw chat --provider edenai --model edenai/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6 -q "Reply with exactly OK."
  OPENCLAW_LIVE_TEST=1 EDENAI_API_KEY="$EDENAI_API_KEY" \
      pnpm test extensions/edenai/edenai.live.test.ts
  ```
- Evidence after fix: see the screenshot/terminal capture attached to the PR. Live `chat/completions` returns `OK`, the live `/v3/models` catalog (500+ rows) is warmed by `prepareDynamicModel` and feeds dynamic resolution with real per-model metadata, and the gated live vitest passes.
- Observed result after fix: provider is selectable from the wizard; `openclaw chat` returns a real assistant reply from multiple underlying vendors via Eden AI; `openclaw models list --provider edenai` shows the curated offline catalog while live discovery powers the runtime model resolution path.
- What was not tested: image generation, audio transcription, TTS, and embeddings (intentionally out of scope for this PR; see Out of scope below). Codex review was not run locally because the contributor does not have Codex access.

## Root Cause (if applicable)

N/A (feature add, not a bug fix).

## Regression Test Plan (if applicable)

- Coverage level that should have caught this:
  - [x] Unit test
  - [ ] Seam / integration test
  - [ ] End-to-end test
  - [ ] Existing coverage already sufficient
- Target test or file: `extensions/edenai/onboard.test.ts`, `extensions/edenai/provider-catalog.test.ts`, `extensions/edenai/edenai.live.test.ts`.
- Scenario the test should lock in: provider registers under id `edenai` with `EDENAI_API_KEY` auth, the static catalog ships exactly eight models with Eden AI's hyphen Anthropic id form, `normalizeEdenaiBaseUrl` canonicalises `/v3` and legacy `/v2` paths, onboard preserves the alias and primary model, and dynamic model resolution hits Eden AI's live `/v3/chat/completions` end to end (gated).
- Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: catalog drift between Eden AI's published model ids and the static fallback is the most likely silent failure; the eight-entry test asserts the hyphen ids verbatim. Base-URL normalisation is the next-most-likely regression as Eden AI's API moves from `/v2` to `/v3`.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

- New auth choice in the onboarding wizard: "Eden AI API key" (group "Eden AI").
- New CLI flag `--edenai-api-key <key>` and direct env var `EDENAI_API_KEY`.
- New model-ref shape `edenai/<vendor>/<model>` (for example `edenai/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6`).
- Anthropic models on Eden AI use the hyphen id form (`claude-opus-4-6`), not the dot form (`claude-opus-4.6`). The bundled catalog uses the hyphen form Eden AI returns; Eden AI rejects the dot form with HTTP 400. Manual `models.providers.edenai.models[].id` entries should follow Eden AI's form, not the upstream vendor's.
- Eden AI wraps `response_format: {"type": "json_object"}` output in a ` ```json ... ``` ` code fence. OpenClaw's parser does not require strict `JSON.parse` on assistant text, so this is cosmetic; consumers that need raw JSON should strip the fence.

## Diagram (if applicable)

```text
Before:
[user]
   |
   v
manual models.providers.edenai = { baseUrl, apiKey, api: "openai-completions", models: [...] }

After:
[user] -> openclaw onboard --auth-choice edenai-api-key
              |
              v
        bundled plugin (extensions/edenai)
              |
              v
        OpenAI-compatible /v3/chat/completions -> 21 underlying vendors
```

## Security Impact (required)

- New permissions/capabilities? No.
- Secrets/tokens handling changed? No - reuses the existing `EDENAI_API_KEY` env var convention via the shared `createProviderApiKeyAuthMethod` helper.
- New/changed network calls? Yes - outbound `GET https://api.edenai.run/v3/models` (during live catalog discovery) and the standard `POST /v3/chat/completions` for inference. Both go to a single host suffix (`api.edenai.run`).
- Command/tool execution surface changed? No.
- Data access scope changed? No - users explicitly opt in by setting their own key.
- If any `Yes`, explain risk + mitigation: the network calls share the same SSRF guard, timeout, and error handling that every other OpenAI-compatible provider plugin uses (via `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`). Eden AI's endpoint is publicly documented and the only outbound host is `api.edenai.run`.

## Repro + Verification

### Environment

- OS: Linux x86_64 (also exercised on macOS arm64).
- Runtime/container: Node v22.22.2, pnpm 11.1.0.
- Model/provider: `edenai` (default model `edenai/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6`).
- Integration/channel (if any): n/a (provider plugin only).
- Relevant config (redacted): `EDENAI_API_KEY=ek_...` in `~/.openclaw/.env`.

### Steps

1. `pnpm build && pnpm check && pnpm test extensions/edenai/`
2. `pnpm openclaw onboard --non-interactive --auth-choice edenai-api-key --edenai-api-key "$EDENAI_API_KEY"`
3. `pnpm openclaw models list --provider edenai`
4. `pnpm openclaw chat --provider edenai --model edenai/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6 -q "Reply with exactly OK."`

### Expected

- `pnpm check` clean (typecheck, oxlint, contract checks).
- `pnpm test extensions/edenai` shows 6 unit tests passing (live test skipped when `OPENCLAW_LIVE_TEST` is unset).
- Step 2 prints the configured provider and selected default model.
- Step 3 prints the eight bundled static entries plus the full live catalog when the key resolves.
- Step 4 returns `OK` (or `OK.`/`OK!`).

### Actual

- `pnpm check` clean (lint, typecheck, runtime sidecar guard, dependency pin guard, runtime import cycles - all green).
- `pnpm test:extension edenai` -> 2 test files, 6 tests passing in \~4 s; live test correctly skipped.
- Live chat with `edenai/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6` returns `OK.` - see attached terminal capture.

## Evidence

- [x] Failing test/log before + passing after (new vitest files; no prior coverage to compare against).
- [ ] Trace/log snippets
- [x] Screenshot/recording (terminal capture of `openclaw chat --provider edenai`, attached as a PR comment because GitHub does not let contributors inline-attach artifacts in the description).
- [ ] Perf numbers (if relevant)

## Human Verification (required)

What you personally verified (not just CI):

- Verified scenarios: `openclaw onboard --auth-choice edenai-api-key` flow with a real key; `models list --provider edenai` against the live catalog; `chat` with `edenai/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6` reaching Eden AI and getting an assistant reply.
- Edge cases checked: missing key falls back to the static eight-model catalog (no network); `EDENAI_API_KEY=invalid` surfaces the upstream HTTP 401 cleanly through OpenClaw's standard provider error path.
- What you did **not** verify: image-generation, audio, TTS, and embeddings capabilities (deliberately out of scope; see "Out of scope" in the diagram block).

## Review Conversations

- [x] I replied to or resolved every bot review conversation I addressed in this PR.
- [x] I left unresolved only the conversations that still need reviewer or maintainer judgment.

## Compatibility / Migration

- Backward compatible? Yes - additive only.
- Config/env changes? Yes - new optional env var `EDENAI_API_KEY` and CLI flag `--edenai-api-key`; both unset by default and have no effect on existing setups.
- Migration needed? No.
- If yes, exact upgrade steps: n/a.

## Risks and Mitigations

- Risk: Eden AI's live `/v3/models` catalog includes ids that are not yet in the static fallback list. The static list (eight curated entries) only fires when `EDENAI_API_KEY` is unset.
  - Mitigation: `resolveDynamicModel` accepts any `edenai/<vendor>/<model>` id and synthesises a `ProviderRuntimeModel` with sensible defaults if the live catalog hasn't been fetched yet. Behavior matches OpenRouter's `resolveDynamicModel` path.
- Risk: future Eden AI gateway updates could move endpoints again (the plugin already handles the `/v2` -> `/v3` rename via `normalizeEdenaiBaseUrl`).
  - Mitigation: tests assert the canonical and known-legacy base URLs both normalise to `/v3`. Adding a new legacy variant is a single-line change.

## Out of scope (follow-ups)

- Embeddings via `registerEmbeddingProvider` (Eden AI exposes `/v3/embeddings`).
- Image generation via `registerImageGenerationProvider` (`/v3/image/generations`).
- Audio transcription via `registerMediaUnderstandingProvider({ capabilities: ["audio"] })` (`/v3/audio/transcriptions`).
- Text-to-speech via `registerSpeechProvider` (`/v3/audio/speech`).
- Reasoning policy (`resolveThinkingProfile`): Eden AI does not currently forward Anthropic's `thinking` budget or OpenAI's reasoning-effort knob in a uniform way. Defer until Eden AI exposes the parameter.

The Matrix QA migration still leaves a temporary compatibility plugin, private
